```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

Export a panel as a 3D model for another application, or save a projected
figure with editable paths and source-row information. This article writes
both kinds of output from small plots. Installation is covered in
[Get started](ggplot3d.html). Optional bridges use
[rgl](https://dmurdoch.github.io/rgl/), an R package for interactive 3D scenes,
and [rayrender](https://www.rayrender.net), an R path tracer.

## Example

The built-in motor-car data record weight in thousands of pounds, fuel
economy in miles per US gallon and gross horsepower. Model names provide
hover text and selection keys. Start with a view of these three variables.

```{r cars, fig.alt="Motor cars positioned by weight, fuel economy and horsepower."}
cars <- data.frame(mtcars, model = rownames(mtcars))
p <- ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp, tooltip = model, data_id = model)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d() + labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg", z = "horsepower")
p
```

## Model files

`export_3d()` writes one panel, selected by its index in layout order.
The extension chooses the format. The following example writes a binary
glTF model, called a GLB file, to a temporary directory and checks the file.

```{r model-file}
out <- tempfile("ggplot3d-export-")
dir.create(out)
glb <- file.path(out, "cars.glb")
export_3d(p, glb)
file.info(glb)$size > 0
```

The glTF 2.0 format transfers meshes, mapped vertex colours, materials and a
camera to applications such as Blender. Each layer becomes a named node,
so it can be selected and restyled after import. The plot's vertical axis
becomes positive y. An oblique camera is exported as an orthographic camera
along its viewing direction.

Keep companion files together when copying an export. Text is omitted from
these model formats, and dashed paths become solid. Panes, grid lines and
box edges are included with `furniture = TRUE`.

| Extension | Contents | Companion file |
|---|---|---|
| `.glb` | glTF scene and buffer in one binary file | None |
| `.gltf` | glTF scene description | `.bin` buffer |
| `.ply` | Binary vertices, normals, colours and faces; optional edges | None |
| `.obj` | Objects, vertices, colours and faces | `.mtl` materials |
| `.stl` | Binary triangles | None |

Write the other formats with the same call. The temporary directory makes
every example runnable without choosing an output folder first.

```{r formats}
formats <- c("gltf", "ply", "obj", "stl")
for (extension in formats) {
  export_3d(p, file.path(out, paste0("cars.", extension)))
}
list.files(out)
```

## Scale and primitive choices

Model coordinates follow the aspect-scaled panel box. Its longest side is
`size` file units long; expanded scale limits also contribute to that box.
PLY and STL use positive z as the vertical axis. OBJ uses positive y.
The format's units are interpreted by the importing application.

Paths become closed tubes with their drawn width as diameter, and markers
become small solids. Width and height set the layout used to convert physical
line and point sizes relative to the box. Use line and point primitives when
the receiving format and software support them.

```{r primitive-options}
export_3d(p, file.path(out, "points.ply"), points = "point")
export_3d(p, file.path(out, "large.stl"), size = 50,
  lines = "tube", points = "mesh")
file.info(file.path(out, c("points.ply", "large.stl")))$size > 0
```

STL requires tube paths and mesh points because it stores triangles only.
Exporting a surface to STL transfers its triangles; closing the entire model
for manufacturing is a separate modelling step. Traced SDF and volume layers
produce images in the plot. Use their mesh-producing surface counterparts
when exporting model geometry, as shown in
[Ray marching and volumes](ray-marching.html).

## Animated glTF

`animate_3d()` writes camera translation, rotation and zoom tracks to glTF.
The first panel is exported. Start with a three-frame turn of the same motor
cars; the result records the file and frame count.

```{r animated-camera}
turn <- animate_3d(p, azimuth = c(-60, -20, 20), frames = 3,
  file = file.path(out, "turn.glb"), fps = 2, width = 320, height = 320,
  workers = 1, progress = FALSE)
turn$frame_count
```

For changing data, a time column selects the rows drawn in each frame.
Scales train on all frames, and visibility tracks select the frame's geometry
in the file. Here the horsepower coordinate increases by twenty in the
second frame. These changed coordinates are an illustration of animation.

```{r animated-data}
states <- rbind(transform(cars, step = 1),
  transform(cars, step = 2, hp = hp + 20))
changing <- ggplot(states, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
motion <- animate_3d(changing, time = "step", azimuth = -60,
  file = file.path(out, "states.gltf"), fps = 2,
  width = 320, height = 320, workers = 1, progress = FALSE)
motion$frame_count
```

Keep a projection type fixed within an animation. Camera paths and frame
timing are described in [Camera animation and interaction](motion.html).

## rgl meshes and scenes

The rgl bridge dispatches through its own generic functions. Convert the
plot to a mesh with vertex colours, then inspect the vertex and triangle
counts. Point primitives can instead populate the mesh's point indices.

```{r rgl-mesh}
mesh <- rgl::as.mesh3d(p)
c(vertices = ncol(mesh$vb), triangles = ncol(mesh$it))
```

Draw with the plot's camera angles and projection through `rgl::plot3d()`.
This example uses rgl's null device so it also runs during document builds.
rgl centres the drawn geometry itself, so its framing may differ from the
original plot. The scene includes text through rgl's native text primitives.

```{r rgl-scene}
old <- options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)
ids <- rgl::plot3d(p)
length(ids)
rgl::close3d()
options(old)
```

## rayrender scenes

Build a rayrender scene to continue with that package's materials, lights
and renderer. The bridge creates one diffuse mesh object per nonempty
geometry layer, with the mapped vertex colours. Paths become tubes and points
become solids; translucency is omitted.

```{r rayrender-scene}
scene <- as_rayrender_3d(p)
nrow(scene)
```

Setting `render = TRUE` passes the scene and plot camera to rayrender's
renderer. Additional arguments control that render. The native path tracer
in [Ray marching and volumes](ray-marching.html) provides diffuse rendering
directly within a ggplot panel.

## Semantic SVG

The native Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) writer preserves the connection
between a visible fragment and its source layer and row. Hovering or focusing
a fragment highlights fragments from the same source row, and its title
provides tooltip text. The projected view stays fixed.

```{r semantic-svg}
svg <- file.path(out, "cars.svg")
save_svg_3d(p, svg, interactive = TRUE, width = 624, height = 432)
doc <- xml2::read_xml(svg)
fragments <- xml2::xml_find_all(doc, ".//*[@data-primitive]")
head(unique(xml2::xml_attr(fragments, "data-layer")))
```

Each fragment carries `data-layer`, `data-row` and `data-primitive`
attributes. Consecutive runs from each layer are grouped in paint order,
preserving depth ordering across layers. Clipping paths and compound seam
underlays retain the visibility of the compiled vector scene. Set
`interactive = FALSE` for a file without the hover script.

The embedded preview below retains hover and keyboard interaction. It uses
an HTML object containing the exported SVG itself.

```{r svg-preview, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Semantic SVG of motor cars with linked source-row hover and model-name tooltips."}
bytes <- readBin(svg, "raw", n = file.info(svg)$size)
uri <- paste0("data:image/svg+xml;base64,", jsonlite::base64_enc(bytes))
htmltools::tags$object(data = uri, type = "image/svg+xml",
  width = "100%", height = 432, `aria-label` = "Motor-car SVG with hover",
  "Motor-car scatterplot with weight, mpg and horsepower axes.")
```

Open the SVG directly in a browser or embed it as an HTML object to retain
its interaction. An SVG displayed through an image element supplies a static
preview. [Interactive viewing](viewer.html) provides a camera you can rotate.

## TikZ

TikZ is a LaTeX drawing language. Export the whole projected plot as editable
fill, draw, text and clipping commands. The standalone setting includes a
document preamble; disable it for code to insert into an existing document.

```{r tikz}
tikz <- export_code_3d(p, "tikz", file = file.path(out, "cars.tex"))
cat(paste(head(strsplit(tikz, "\n")[[1]], 5), collapse = "\n"))
```

Compile the file with `pdflatex cars.tex`. The generated code uses TikZ's
`svg.path` library, and TeX selects the text font. Raster colourbars and
annotations become coloured pixel rectangles. The complete figure includes
all panels, furniture and legends.

## Asymptote and PRC

Asymptote is a language for mathematical graphics. Its exporter writes
model-space geometry, materials, text and a camera, which you can edit to
render another view. The panel index selects the scene to export.

```{r asymptote}
asy <- export_code_3d(p, "asy", panel = 1,
  file = file.path(out, "cars.asy"), prc = TRUE)
cat(paste(head(strsplit(asy, "\n")[[1]], 5), collapse = "\n"))
```

The PRC setting requests embedded 3D content in PDF. Compile with
`asy -tex pdflatex -f pdf cars.asy` and install the TeX packages media9 and
ocgx2. A PDF reader with PRC support supplies the interactive view.
For a static PDF or ordinary SVG through an R graphics device, use
[Output backends](backends.html).
